identity.title: EditBench: Evaluating LLM Abilities to Perform Real-World Instructed Code Edits

problem.claim: Evaluate LLMs that modify existing developer code in response to user instructions.

gap.claim: Few benchmarks directly assess instructed code editing, and existing datasets often use artificial sources.

contributions.claim: Introduces EditBench, grounded in user instructions and code contexts collected in the wild.
Provides 545 problems spanning multiple natural and programming languages and use cases from error resolution to feature addition.
Includes context-dependent tasks requiring understanding of code context, highlighted code, and cursor position alongside the instruction.

stated_novelty.claim: The benchmark’s stated distinction is its real-world grounding and explicit evaluation of context-dependent editing conditions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report evaluating 40 diverse LLMs; only 3 models scored above 60%, characterizing EditBench as challenging.
The authors report that performance varies across categories of user instructions.
The authors report that changing contextual information affects task success by up to 11%, highlighting the importance of realistic context evaluation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Instructed code editing is becoming a common AI coding-assistant interaction, but benchmark coverage is limited and often artificial.
EditBench is introduced as a real-world-grounded benchmark with 545 multilingual, varied-use-case problems.
Its problems require models to integrate the instruction with code context, highlighted code, and cursor position.
Evaluation across 40 LLMs reports low overall scores, category-dependent performance, and up to 11% variation from contextual information.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly separates user instructions from several contextual signals and reports up to 11% success-rate variation when context changes.

lessons.interpretation: This suggests that editing benchmarks should treat interaction state as part of the task definition, not merely as optional input.
lessons.application: When designing a code-editing evaluation, factor instruction, surrounding code, highlighted span, and cursor position into controlled context variants and report their separate effects.
lessons.exception: This design may be unsuitable when the target workflow does not expose stable highlighting or cursor state.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the scoring metric, model identities, category definitions, statistical uncertainty, or evaluation protocol.
The reported 11% variation is not qualified by whether it is an absolute or relative change, nor by the exact context conditions.
